## Notes on Numbers 27 — Verse by Verse

### v. 1: The daughters of Zelophehad — their ancestry and names

The daughters are introduced with a full genealogy linking them to Manasseh son of Joseph. In the Ancient Near East, land was normally passed from fathers to sons, not daughters. The issue arises here because the preceding chapter (Numbers 26:52–56) had just set out the distribution of Canaan by male census — which would have excluded these women entirely (Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/). Precept Austin notes that these women showed faith greater than their father’s generation: Israel had not yet conquered any land, yet they believed God’s promise and boldly stepped forward to claim their share (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-27-commentary). Calvin observes that their suit, though about private advantage, arose from a good principle — they treated God’s promise as a certainty, as if they were already demanding to be put in possession (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-27.html).

### v. 2: They stood before Moses, Eleazar, the leaders, and all the congregation

They made their petition at the doorway of the Tent of Meeting — the most public and authoritative venue in the camp. Precept Austin likens this to appearing before the president and congress combined; their courage was remarkable for women in that culture (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-27-commentary). Ellicott notes that they brought their case to the highest tribunal, appealing not only to Moses but to the whole assembly (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm).

### v. 3: “Our father died in the wilderness… not among the followers of Korah… he died because of his own sin, and he had no sons.”

The daughters carefully distinguish their father’s death from that of Korah’s rebels. Why? Because Korah’s family likely lost their inheritance along with their lives (Numbers 16:30, “swallows them up with all that is theirs”). They are arguing that their father suffered no such special judicial forfeiture.

On the phrase “died in his own sin,” there are several readings among the older commentators:
- **Ellicott** reports a Jewish tradition that Zelophehad was the man who gathered sticks on the Sabbath (Numbers 15:32–36). But the “more common interpretation” is that he committed only the ordinary sins of human frailty and died the common death of all men, thus not entailing special punishment on his posterity (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm).
- **Calvin** explicitly rejects the Jewish tradition as “childish nonsense.” He understands “his own sin” as a private sin contrasted with public ignominy — he was not among those whose crimes caused their families to be disinherited. Yet Calvin insists the daughters still hold that death itself is the wages of sin (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-27.html).
- **Wenham** (quoted in Precept Austin and Enduring Word) thinks “his own sin” refers to the sin of the whole nation in refusing to enter the promised land (Numbers 13–14). Zelophehad is acknowledged as at least tacitly having sided with the sceptical spies and therefore sentenced to die in the wilderness (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-27-commentary).

### v. 4: “Why should the name of our father disappear…? Give us property among our father’s brothers.”

Their motive is not greed for land but the perpetuation of their father’s name. Precept Austin notes: “These were loyal daughters who clearly loved their deceased father and sought legal rights in order to honour him” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-27-commentary). Enduring Word adds that without sons to inherit his land and perpetuate his name, there was a real sense in which denying inheritance to Zelophehad’s only descendants was to erase his name (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/).

### v. 5: Moses brought their case before the LORD

Moses did not decide the matter himself. Enduring Word calls this what Moses “should do when faced with a new situation — Moses sought God” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/). Calvin praises Moses’ “pious modesty” — he was not ashamed to confess his ignorance until instructed by God. Calvin adds that rulers today are reminded to have recourse to God in perplexities, and God will instruct them by the Spirit of wisdom if they ask (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-27.html). Precept Austin notes that one mark of a spiritual leader is taking the issue to the LORD first — Moses’ “reflex response” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-27-commentary). Allen (quoted there) observes that the scribes wrote an oversized, darkened *nun* in the Hebrew for “their case,” drawing special attention to the fact that this was an appeal from women.

### vv. 6–7: “The daughters of Zelophehad speak correctly. You certainly must give them property…”

God’s ruling is emphatic. The Hebrew pronoun for “give them” is in the masculine gender — Poole (quoted in Enduring Word) says this was “to show that women in this case should enjoy the man’s privilege, and that the heavenly Canaan, whereof this was a type, did belong no less to women than to men” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/). Precept Austin stresses that God’s response went beyond the daughters’ request: they asked for an *aḥuzzāh* (“landed property”); God granted an *aḥuzzaṯ naḥalāh* (“a hereditary possession”), meaning they could transfer it to their heirs — as though their father had had sons (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-27-commentary).

**Anglican typological reading (Bishop Wordsworth, cited in Ellicott):** The inheritance of Canaan is a figure of the heavenly possession. God’s answer shows that “in Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female” and that women, no less than men, are “heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:28–29) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm).

### vv. 8–11: The statutory ordinance of inheritance

God uses this case to establish a permanent statute. The inheritance order becomes: son → daughter → brothers → father’s brothers → nearest kinsman in the clan. Enduring Word observes, “These laws were made in anticipation — in faith — of coming into the inheritance of land in Canaan” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/).

Calvin notes that though God prefers daughters to all other relatives when there is no male issue, with this single exception of the first degree, He admits none but males to the succession, preserving the usual order. He connects this specifically to the land of Canaan, where the memory of God’s blessing through Abraham and the twelve tribes was to be preserved distinctly (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-27.html).

A practical problem created by this law — that an heiress who married outside her tribe would transfer tribal land — is addressed later in Numbers 36 (Enduring Word; Precept Austin).

### v. 12: “Go up this mountain of the Abarim range and see the land…”

Ellicott remarks on the striking placement of this command immediately after the daughters’ inheritance is secured: “They were to enter into the land of promise… The great lawgiver himself was to be excluded on account of his transgression.” Yet Moses does not shrink from recording his own sentence of exclusion right beside an incident that throws it into greater prominence (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm).

The Pulpit Commentary (excerpted in search results) identifies Abarim as the range behind the Arboth Moab; its northern portion opposite Jericho was called Pisgah, and the highest point was Nebo (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-27.html). Moses had already been told he would not enter the land (Numbers 20:12); here he is granted the consolation of seeing it. Enduring Word notes that Deuteronomy 3:25–27 indicates this favour was given in answer to Moses’ own prayer (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/).

### v. 13: “You too will be gathered to your people, as your brother Aaron was”

Ellicott cross-references Genesis 25:8 (Abraham) and notes that “gathered unto thy people” cannot refer to the place of burial — Moses was buried alone by God (Deuteronomy 34:6) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm). Enduring Word, quoting Cole, explains this as the “Hebrew concept of unity and identity with the faithful forefathers… with whom they would rest and find peace” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/).

### v. 14: The reason: rebellion at the waters of Meribah in Kadesh

God reminds Moses precisely why he is excluded: he “rebelled against My command to show My holiness in their sight regarding the waters.” This refers to Numbers 20:12–13, where Moses struck the rock instead of speaking to it. Enduring Word, quoting Morgan, says: “The account… keeps before us the fact that the most faithful servants of God cannot escape the results of their failure in this life” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/).

### vv. 15–16: Moses appeals: “May the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man…”

Moses’ response to his own death sentence is remarkable. Ellicott calls it “a remarkable instance of the true greatness of Moses, as a type of Him whose words were, ‘Weep not for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children’ (Luke 23:28).” Instead of grief or remorse, Moses’ mind was fixed on the welfare of the people. He does not appoint his own sons or a man of his own choice but commits the matter entirely to God (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm).

Calvin draws out the significance of the title “God of the spirits of all flesh”: Moses is saying there must be someone ready in God’s hand to be appointed, since God fashions and refashions the men He chooses as His ministers and supplies them with the faculties they require. Calvin adds: “When we are deprived of good rulers, they should be sought from the Maker Himself, whose special gift the power of good government is” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-27.html).

**Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Guzik quotes Adam Clarke: “This must certainly mean the Spirit of God; and because he was endued with this Spirit, therefore he was capable of leading the people. How miserably qualified is that man for the work of God who is not guided and influenced by the Holy Ghost!” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/).

### v. 17: “Who will go out and come in before them… so that the congregation will not be like sheep without a shepherd.”

Ellicott explains that “going out and coming in” denotes ordinary daily life (Deuteronomy 28:6; 31:2), while “leading out and bringing in” — like a shepherd with his flock — denotes the direction of the conduct of others (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm). Enduring Word notes that sheep without a shepherd are in constant danger — trouble finding food and water, wandering into dangerous places. The image is fulfilled ultimately in Jesus the Good Shepherd (John 10:11), and in an additional sense in the New Testament office of pastor-teacher (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/).

### v. 18: “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man with the Spirit in him, and lay your hands on him.”

**On “the Spirit”:** The Hebrew lacks the definite article. Ellicott says it “appears to denote spiritual endowment and qualifications” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm). The Pulpit Commentary insists “it can only mean the Holy Spirit, as in Numbers 11:25 sq.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-27.html). Constable (quoted via StudyLight) notes, “This spirit was not something that now came upon Joshua… it already existed in Joshua and was the basis of God’s choice of him. Deuteronomy 34:9 applies the phrase ‘full of the spirit of Wisdom’ to Joshua, confirming the thought here” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/27-23.html).

**On the laying on of hands:** Calvin treats this as a “solemn rite of consecration.” It was used before the Law (the patriarchs blessed their sons this way), for priestly inauguration, and by the apostles for appointing pastors. Moses laid hands on Joshua to testify publicly that Joshua was no longer his own master but dedicated to God. Calvin also holds that new grace was conferred through the laying on of hands — citing 2 Timothy 1:6 as a parallel — though Joshua already had spiritual gifts (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-27.html). Ellicott concurs: “It seems that special qualifications for the office were bestowed in connection with the imposition of the hands of Moses, for it is written in Deuteronomy 34:9 that ‘Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands upon him’” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm).

**Enduring Word** lists Joshua’s many qualifications: he led the army against Amalek (Exodus 17), served as Moses’ assistant (Exodus 24), helped at the tabernacle after the golden calf (Exodus 33), was zealous for Moses’ authority (Numbers 11), and was one of the two faith-filled spies (Numbers 13–14). Above all, he was “a man in whom is the Spirit” — the most important qualification of all (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/).

### v. 19: “Have him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation, and commission him in their sight.”

The public nature of the commissioning is essential — it confirms for all Israel that Joshua is God’s choice, not Moses’ personal preference. Ellicott cross-references Deuteronomy 31:23, where Moses gives Joshua the charge: “Be strong and of a good courage” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm).

### v. 20: “Confer on him some of your authority, so that the whole congregation of Israel will obey him.”

Enduring Word sees this as an immediate sharing of authority — a transitional period of some months where Joshua led alongside Moses (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/). Calvin explains the word translated “authority” (or “honour” in the KJV) as signifying not just external splendour but spiritual honour by which God commands reverence towards His servants. Moses was not stripped of his own gifts; rather, “without diminution of his own gifts, he made the person who was about to be his successor his associate in their possession” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-27.html).

### v. 21: “He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who will seek counsel for him before the LORD by the judgment of the Urim.”

**This verse marks a critical difference between Moses and Joshua.** The Pulpit Commentary states: “Moses was as much above the priests as he was above the tribe princes; but Joshua was only the civil and military head of the nation, and was as much subordinate to the high priest in one way as the high priest was subordinate to him in another” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-27.html). Ellicott likewise: whereas Moses received direct revelation from God (Numbers 12:8), Joshua would receive divine guidance through Eleazar the priest by means of Urim and Thummim (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm).

Constable (via StudyLight) adds that “only rarely did the Lord speak to Joshua directly” — Joshua functioned differently from Moses throughout his leadership (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/27-23.html).

**Calvin’s Reformed emphasis:** Joshua is “subordinated to the priest on one point” — consulting God by the Urim and Thummim. “In all legitimate dominion religion ought surely to hold the first place; for, since all things depend upon God, it is absurd that they should be separated from His service” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-27.html). The civil leader must seek God through the priestly channel; religion holds primacy.

**The Pulpit Commentary** adds that the actual nature of the Urim and Thummim “is not told us in Scripture, and has left no reliable trace in the tradition of the Jews; it must, therefore, remain for ever an insoluble mystery.” Its real use belonged to “the dark ages of Israel, after the light of Moses had set, and before the light of the prophets had arisen” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-27.html).

### vv. 22–23: Moses did as the LORD commanded — he laid hands on Joshua and commissioned him.

Moses’ obedience is immediate and complete. Enduring Word emphasises that the public presentation and laying on of hands “presented Joshua before all Israel as the next leader, the one who should expect to follow as God’s appointed leader” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/). Calvin concludes that Moses did all this “so that all might be fully assured that God would rule, no less than before, in the person of Joshua” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-27.html).

## Differences Among Protestant Traditions

### On the nature of the Spirit in Joshua (v. 18)

- **Reformed (Calvin):** The “spirit” refers to eminent gifts — intelligence, judgment, magnanimity, skill in war — a metonymy for the gifts that proceed from the Spirit. The laying on of hands confers new grace for office (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-27.html).
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word, quoting Adam Clarke):** Strong emphasis that the Spirit here “must certainly mean the Spirit of God” and that without the Holy Spirit’s guidance no one is qualified for God’s work. The focus is on the Spirit’s empowerment for ministry (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/).
- **Older Anglican (Ellicott/Pulpit):** The Pulpit Commentary insists the reference can “only mean the Holy Spirit, as in Numbers 11:25 sq.”; Ellicott is more cautious, noting the missing definite article and describing it as “spiritual endowment and qualifications” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm).

### On the relationship of civil and religious authority (v. 21)

- **Reformed (Calvin):** The prince must consult God by the mouth of the priest. “In all legitimate dominion religion ought surely to hold the first place.” This reflects the Reformed emphasis on the spiritual authority’s role in guiding the civil magistrate — though Calvin also held that civil and ecclesiastical spheres are distinct, here the priestly channel is indispensable for divine guidance (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-27.html).
- **Older Anglican (Pulpit):** Notes that “in after times no doubt the political headship quite overpowered and overshadowed the ecclesiastical, but this does not seem to have been so intended.” There is a hint of a normative pattern of balanced powers (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-27.html).
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik):** The emphasis is less on institutional subordination and more on the practical point that “the priests would support Joshua’s leadership.” Guzik does not stress a hierarchy of priest over ruler but a partnership (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/).

### On the application to women in the church (vv. 1–11)

- **Evangelical (Precept Austin):** Draws a specific application to Christian sisters: though the woman’s position in the church is one of subjection, “this should not mean that her enjoyment of the spiritual inheritance should in any way be lessened.” A sister “is certainly not a silent nonentity in a seat” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-27-commentary).
- **Anglican (Ellicott/Wordsworth):** The typological reading focuses on the heavenly inheritance — the passage shows that in Christ “there is neither male nor female” (Galatians 3:28–29) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/27.htm).
- **Baptist (Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik):** The daughters are examples of those who “boldly approached to receive an inheritance by faith” — an evangelistic application urging sinners to go “straight away to Jesus” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-27/).

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

**Case law development:** Both Constable (via StudyLight) and Allen (quoted in Precept Austin) note that Numbers 27 illustrates how case law developed in Israel. When a situation not covered by existing laws arose, the people went to Moses, who inquired of God. The revelation then became precedent (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-27-commentary; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/27-23.html).

**Peake’s Commentary** (via StudyLight) suggests that between the announcement of Moses’ death (Numbers 27:12–14) and the account of its occurrence, “not only the rest of Nu. but the whole of Dt. intervene, this being due to the arrangement of the Pentateuch… by the final compiler.” It also notes that the laying on of hands, while symbolical in the final text, “originally such physical contact was probably thought to be a magical means of conveying special powers” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/numbers-27.html).
